papers.title: Edge-Optimized YOLOv11n Architecture for Offline Recognition of Nigerian Sign Language Alphanumeric Gestures
papers.abstract: Deaf inclusion across sub-Saharan society faces regional hurdles, with Nigeria as the core empirical focus. Existing recognition models demand heavy computational infrastructure. However, standard mobile phones used locally rarely exceed 1 GB to 4 GB of RAM. This study addresses constraints through a lightweight YOLO11n object-detection framework. The system provides real-time Nigerian Sign Language recognition for low-resource hardware. A benchmark dataset containing 11,208 raw gesture images was established. The data spans 33 static classes collected from five signers. Partitioning isolates signers S1 through S3 for training. Signer S4 provides validation data. Signer S5 is reserved for testing. Spatial augmentations are restricted strictly to the training set. This yields 23,509 training images. The validation and test sets each maintain 1,681 images across varied environments. The framework integrates a quantization-aware compression objective. Loss functions merge with squared Frobenius-norm penalties to govern weight distortion. A Spatial-Density Occlusion Index quantifies background complexity and self-occlusion. A latency-profiling equation relates floating-point operations and memory bandwidth to chipset clock speed. Performance testing on physical Android hardware utilizes unquantized FP32 weights. Mean inference latencies span 405.5 ms to 1,759.4 ms. Measured against test data, the algorithm attains a Precision of 0.9975. Recall reaches 0.9991. Mean Average Precision is 0.9942. Outcomes support offline functionality on constrained mobile devices. Practical deployment operates through a mobile utility using CameraX. The application captures gestures in real time. Recognized signs display as text instantly.

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of Live Intraoperative Surgical Expert Narrations
papers.abstract: Manual annotation remains the principal bottleneck in surgical video understanding. Live intraoperative narration by the operating surgeon is a scalable alternative that requires no manual annotation, but the information it contains has not been characterized. We analyzed 13 endoscopic lumbar spine decompression procedures (13.2 h) by two senior spine surgeons, using time-synchronized close-mic German audio. An annotation-free pipeline (word-level speech recognition, deterministic correction of surgical-term errors, utterance fusion, LLM-based translation to English, and relevance filtering) converted speech into time-stamped procedural cues labelled with the surgical entities they reference and their speech act. Of 3,171 utterances, 1,201 (37.9%) were retained as procedural cues, while 57.6% were non-procedural and removed. Retained cues referenced instruments (60.7%), anatomy (48.0%) and surgical actions (57.1%), and 98.5% carried at least one of these. 39% of cues (472 of 1,201) were directives, mainly instrument requests and commands. All 467 manually verified instrument requests preceded the instrument's appearance in the field, by a median of 8.2 s. Domain-term transcription corruption affected 18.0% of retained cues. Live narration is thus a dense, annotation-free supervisory signal describing instruments, anatomy, actions and team coordination, but it is noisy and temporally displaced from the events it names, and this displacement must be modelled before safe downstream use.

papers.title: When frequency domain classification is superior to spatial
papers.abstract: Modern image classification models largely rely on local characteristics and feature extraction for their predictions. This focused approach works well in the spatial domain, but reportedly falls short in the frequency domain, even though both representations contain the same information. This study demonstrates that the significant reduction in accuracy in the frequency domain stems from the lack of local features. Locally swapping data in the frequency domain significantly decreases its inverse spatial domain accuracy, even below that of the frequency domain; however, the frequency domain accuracy remains relatively constant. Moreover, the use of datasets containing global features in the spatial domain yields higher accuracy in the frequency domain. Using these results, a hybrid model is constructed, combining one model trained only in the frequency domain and another trained only in the spatial domain to achieve higher classification accuracy. The proposed visual geometry group (VGG) and vision transformer (ViT) architectures are trained on the ImageNet-100, WikiArt, DTD, FMD, PSVRT, and KTH-TIPS2-b datasets and evaluated.

papers.title: From Zero to OCR: A Data-Centric Framework for Unsupported Low-Resource Scripts
papers.abstract: Optical character recognition (OCR) remains inaccessible to many low-resource scripts because annotated document images are unavailable and synthetic training data can fail to preserve script-specific visual structure. We present a data-centric framework that builds end-to-end OCR for such scripts from only an unannotated text corpus and digital fonts, without manually annotating a single training image. A synthetic data engine renders word, line and page images with correct complex-script shaping and automatically derived labels; a YOLOv8 word detector and a convolutional recurrent recognizer trained with connectionist temporal classification learn from these images; and a stage-gate evaluation protocol isolates recognition error before detection is introduced. We demonstrate the framework on Kashmiri, a Perso-Arabic Nastaliq script with approximately 6.8 million speakers that none of six widely used OCR engines supports. Three line-level recognizers, including one transferred from Arabic, stalled between 41% and 79% character error rate (CER), motivating a word-level formulation; subsequent improvements came primarily from rendering fidelity, diacritic-preserving crop margins and tuned non-maximum suppression. The resulting system achieves 0.39% CER on held-out words, 10.0% on synthetic pages and 13.5% on browser-rendered digital pages, and establishes reference results of 18.45% on typeset book pages and 49.8% on degraded historical documents. We publicly release the trained models, the inference code and a synthetic dataset of 285,864 Kashmiri text-line images, and we describe a step-by-step procedure for building OCR for other unsupported scripts.

papers.title: HistGramBench: Measuring Structural Recovery When Multimodal Models Redraw Historical Mathematical Diagrams as TikZ
papers.abstract: Digital libraries preserve mathematical books printed from the sixteenth to the twentieth century, but the lettered diagrams in them, the figures on which Euclidean proofs depend, remain scanned images whose content cannot be searched. Redrawing such a diagram as a short drawing program would record which points lie on which lines and circles. But a printed plate offers no source code against which the redrawing could be checked. We introduce HistGramBench, a benchmark of 2,507 diagrams from 95 works printed between 1551 and 1933 in eight languages. For each diagram, two AI models from different providers agree on the facts a reader takes from the figure, such as which lines are parallel or where two lines meet, and every redrawing is checked against those facts on the model's own drawing. We evaluate six affordable AI models. The best recovers about three fifths of these facts, and most of what the models miss comes from programs that never produce a drawing. Parallels and tangencies are the hardest relations to reproduce. HistGramBench gives historians and librarians a way to measure when such tools can make old mathematical diagrams searchable.

papers.title: From Fragmentation to Fusion: A Survey and Roadmap for Omnimodal Embeddings
papers.abstract: Embedding models underpin virtually every modern AI system, from search engines to recommendation systems. Despite shared mathematical foundations, research on embedding models remains fragmented by modality: the communities develop largely in isolation, seldom exchanging insights. We argue that this fragmentation obscures a deeper convergence. Driven by contrastive learning, Transformer architectures, and a granularity shift, embedding research across modalities is converging toward a common set of principles, even as modality-specific challenges remain underexplored. To reason across this convergence without conflating it, we propose a framework of three progressively harder capabilities: coverage, comparability, and compositionality. Three paths toward unification satisfy these in turn: transformation broadens coverage, alignment enables comparability, and joint embedding, the terminus we advocate, aims at compositionality. This position paper traces the resulting evolution, providing the first unified, cross-cutting treatment of omnimodal embedding research.

papers.title: MEMENTO: Learning Context Management for Long Context Processing Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents that operate over long inputs must perform context management: deciding what to retain in a fixed-size context window. A common approach is compaction, where the model replaces its history with a self-generated note. Yet off-the-shelf agentic models, including GPT-5.5 and GLM-5.3, often write ineffective notes, and reinforcement learning (RL) alone rarely discovers useful note-taking behavior. We present MEMENTO, a long-context agent built on Qwen3-8B and trained to manage its context through compaction. We first bootstrap note-taking by fine-tuning on synthetic trajectories annotated with notes generated in hindsight, then reinforce it with RL using a reward that combines answer correctness, note-quality heuristics, and confidence calibration. Although trained only to compact into a fresh window, MEMENTO extends at test time to strategies such as context folding and confidence-based backtracking. On book-level question answering across four benchmarks, with books of up to 2.5M tokens, MEMENTO raises Qwen3-8B's accuracy from 36.9% to 67.8% while never holding more than 20K tokens in context. It outperforms GPT-5.5 agent in the same harness (13.1%) and full book context (56.7%) at less than 1/50 the cost. It also nearly matches a ~100x larger GLM-5.3 agent (69.3%) at 1/9 the cost, and comes within 6.4 points of GLM-5.3 full context at 1/26 the cost.

papers.title: Cross-Lingual Persona Effects in LLM Negotiation
papers.abstract: Tell an LLM negotiator to be "headstrong" and it should hold firm on price, but does that instruction retain the same behavior in every language? To test this, we use identical buyer and seller instances of Gemini 3.6 Flash to negotiate the same 12 CraigslistBargain scenarios in English and Korean. The pilot-scale 2 x 2 x 3 design crosses interaction language, seller urgency (none or strong), and buyer persona (cooperative, neutral, or headstrong), yielding 432 attempted negotiations. We call this property cross-lingual social-policy fidelity: whether a prompt-defined social policy produces the same behavioral effect regardless of interaction language. It often does not. Korean negotiations reached agreement far more often than English (77.3% vs. 52.5%, a 24.8-point gap, Holm-adjusted p = .0039), but only for neutral and headstrong buyers; cooperative buyers were already near-ceiling in both languages. Buyers' opening offers barely differed by language; the gap instead emerged later, through larger seller concessions and a smaller final gap in Korean, and agreed prices were also lower in Korean. Repeating the full design with Qwen3.7 Flash as both agents gives directional support: agreement was again higher in Korean (+13.9 points vs. Gemini's +24.8, with an interval whose lower bound is near zero), and sellers again conceded more. Pragmatic analysis reveals why: while both languages frequently featured face-threatening acts like rejections and counter-offers, Korean dialogue softened these threats with substantially more politeness mitigation, especially among sellers (11.7% vs. 3.6%). These results show that such a policy can produce different simulated negotiation behavior, not just different wording, when only the interaction language changes.

papers.title: Decentralized Multi-Agent Coordination and Communication in Shared Codebases
papers.abstract: Coding agents working in shared repositories may receive separate, independently-motivated requests from human developers, creating a setting that is multi-agent by necessity. When this scenario happens, their individual implementations may work separately but conflict when combined. To study this setting, we introduce ParallACT, a benchmark of orchestrator-free multi-agent coding tasks. ParallACT contains both complementary and contradictory tasks. In complementary tasks, each agent's task is separately useful and implementations must share an interface to be productively combined. In contradictory pairs, both agents' tasks require editing the same code in incompatible ways, and naively combining independent solutions fails to produce a useful implementation. We compare a single-agent oracle given the combined set of tasks against multi-agent settings that vary execution order, visibility, awareness of other agents, and access to a communication channel. We find that the oracle solves most tasks while parallel agents perform substantially worse. Their performance drop is notable for complementary tasks, and particularly sharp for contradictory tasks (e.g., from 62% to 16% for Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.8) where merged code typically satisfies only one specification, and the same gap appears in all six further configurations pairing two agent harnesses with three open-weight models. Simply telling an agent that a peer exists does not help significantly, and giving agents access to a communication channel recovers only a small part of the performance, at an additional token cost. ParallACT thus identifies and isolates a core challenge that will become more common as multi-agent coding by independent principals becomes standard, and provides a controlled test of which coordination strategies help, and at what cost.

papers.title: GAVAGAI: Referential Alignment for Infant-Scale Vision-Language Models via Balanced Optimal Transport
papers.abstract: A child learns which words name which things from roughly 100 million words of input. Vision-language models trained at a comparable scale bind words to referents far less reliably, and we argue that part of the gap is structural: the usual next-token captioning objective has no variable standing for "this word refers to that region," so training applies no direct pressure to ground words. We add such a variable by treating each scene as a small assignment problem between the content words heard and the regions seen, solved as entropic optimal transport under two constraints. First, a word may be assigned to a special NOTHING column instead of any region, which matters because most content words in caregiver speech do not name anything visible. Second, no region may receive more than a bounded share of the assignment mass, a capacity constraint that encodes mutual exclusivity. The alignment step costs about eight Sinkhorn iterations, small next to the vision encoder. In controlled simulation, the naive version of the idea, a row-wise softmax that forces every word onto some region, collapses to 0.000 word-to-picture accuracy under realistic non-reference rates, below the 0.058 of captioning alone, while our two constraints reach 0.075 in that regime and 0.700 on clean input. A one-parameter version of the model reproduces adult cross-situational learning accuracy across three ambiguity conditions (RMSE 0.024). On the SAYCam infant video corpus, adding the alignment loss to a next-token captioning model raises word-to-picture accuracy from 32.4% to 48.7% and localization IoU from 0.18 to 0.38. A contrastive model trained on the same child's data remains stronger on its own benchmark, so our claim is that the loss improves a captioning objective under high non-reference rates, not that it sets a new best.

papers.title: Queering the Audits: Community-Based Auditing of AI Harms to Queer Communities
papers.abstract: AI systems embed majority-group defaults into training data, evaluation metrics, and category definitions, producing documented harms for queer communities including erasure, misclassification, and discrimination. Standard technical audits often rely on aggregate measures and cannot detect harms that be come visible only through the lived experience of affected communities. We conducted a participatory auditing workshop at EurIPS 2025 where 16 queer community members audited four case studies using the 4Cs harm taxonomy (Content, Conduct, Contact, Contract) applied across the AI lifecycle. Participants used structured worksheets and plenary synthesis to classify harms and trace them to their origins in the development pipeline. Across all four cases, participants traced harms to problem definition and data collection, and they identified contractual structures that extract value from vulnerable populations while providing minimal recourse. These findings illustrate that community-informed auditing surfaces concrete, identity-specific harms that aggregate evaluation methods risk overlooking.

papers.title: Cross-Prompt Reuse of Entity-Replacement Responses
papers.abstract: With model weights fixed, we measure how much of an entity-replacement response transfers between English factual questions, beyond whether answers change. We add the hidden-state change from two source questions to a target question about the same entity, comparing the predicted log-probability shift between two relations' published answers, given known answer prefixes, with the measured one. Hidden reuse injects the aligned change at 50% depth before the target's remaining layers; direct reuse adds source output-score changes. With other-relation sources, hidden reuse removes 45% and 49% of no-change error on 0.5-1B Qwen and Llama. Gemma-2-2B removes 22% and passes one of three comparisons in plain text without its default beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token. A later protocol restoring it yields 58-68%, passing every comparison on three cohorts. Larger checkpoints, chat format and new entities show replication and format- or cohort-dependent failures. On small plain-format checkpoints, other-relation hidden reuse mainly reproduces the shift both relations' questions share, without reliably lowering relation-selective error. With target-relation sources, hidden reuse's post hoc advantage over direct reuse is 0.2-0.9 nats outside chat format, unconfirmed and not replacement-specific. The same relation-neutral change at both questions' entity tokens lowers relation-selective error more than random or other-replacement changes, indicating receiving-question dependence.

papers.title: Humanized but Still True? Auditing Facts and Detection in AI-Text Humanizers
papers.abstract: AI "humanizers" rewrite machine-generated text so that detectors classify it as human-written. Public leaderboards score evasion and embedding similarity, but not whether checkable details survive. We check whether numbers, dates, person and organization names, and quoted spans survive each rewrite, using a rule-based checker validated by two AI annotators (precision 0.84-1.00, recall 0.93-0.95; no human annotation). In the October 2026 cycle of a public humanizer leaderboard, all 11 commercial tools changed or dropped at least one of these units in 35-65% of the documents that contained one. Most changes were to quoted spans; counting numbers and names alone, 10 of the 11 tools still altered at least one in 20% or more of the documents. The September 2026 cycle was similar (19-50%). An open 12B humanizer kept at least 97% of numbers and names in fact-dense U.S. federal agency text, but reworded 67-78% of the quoted spans, against its own prompt. Unit retention and detector evasion were not clearly related across tools (Spearman rho = -0.46, 95% CI -0.65 to 0.08), and the open model's four released files (two of them quantization-aware low-bit files) did not show the pre-registered monotone trade-off. On federal texts with matched human, AI-styled and humanized versions, a general-purpose decision model, Jev, asked a single zero-shot question, separated human originals from humanized rewrites with AUROC 0.864 (0.827-0.902), 0.18-0.22 higher than Binoculars, Fast-DetectGPT and the adversarially trained RADAR, while calling 24% of the human originals AI at a 0.5 threshold. On the AI-styled rewrites by 2026 models, both perplexity-based detectors scored below chance (AUROC 0.37 and 0.39), also with line breaks removed. Hypotheses, data rules and analyses were frozen before the main runs; two earlier data contacts are disclosed. We release the checker and the per-item results.

papers.title: LF-VideoQA: Evaluating Long-Video Understanding with Long-Form Theory-of-Mind Questions
papers.abstract: The hardest part of understanding a long video is not pinpointing any one moment but synthesizing many, e.g., answering a question that requires tracking what develops across hours of content and articulating how the pieces fit together. To date, most long-video QA datasets require only a short answer or a multiple-choice selection, oversimplifying the long-video understanding task to retrieval. We introduce LF-VideoQA, a dataset for long-form, open-ended question answering over long narrative videos built on theory-of-mind questions: a character's belief depends on everything they have seen or been told, so each question demands assembling and reasoning from evidence distributed across the video. The dataset contains more than 6,300 questions on 94 recent films; each requires reasoning over scenes spanning an average of 23 minutes and comes with a question-specific rubric for recall and precision scoring. The dataset is created entirely automatically by annotating screenplays with scene events and each character's first-order beliefs and meta-beliefs, then generating (question, answer, rubric) triples through LLM-based question generation and verification; human studies validate their quality. We evaluate four families of state-of-the-art open-source VLMs across three settings and find the task highly challenging: (i) even an oracle with access to the screenplay falls well short of complete answers; (ii) the best non-oracle model attains barely half of the recall level of the oracle; (iii) unlike on prior long-video benchmarks, captions and subtitles underperform the video itself, indicating that the questions need visual evidence; and (iv) recall is the predominant bottleneck, with answers omitting many required rubric claims.

papers.title: Circuit Oracle: Automating Attribution Graph Analysis via Natural-Language Queries
papers.abstract: Attribution graphs, an emerging tool in mechanistic interpretability, use transcoders to decompose language model computations into sparse interpretable features connected by causal edges. However, turning a graph into a safety-relevant insight requires hours of manual analysis by experts. We introduce Circuit Oracle, an off-the-shelf LLM equipped with a multi-agent harness and task-specific authored skills, which answers natural-language questions about a target model by reading the attribution graph through tool calls. We evaluate it on three safety-relevant proxy tasks: detecting spurious features in probe circuits, eliciting hidden knowledge from taboo-finetuned models, and suppression jailbreaking via feature-level interventions. Beyond task scores, the oracle produces pruned subgraphs and context-specific feature explanations that we assess qualitatively. Results are mixed. On spurious-feature detection, Circuit Oracle reaches 78.2 $\pm$ 2.4% accuracy, outperforming single-layer feature-ranking baselines. On secret elicitation, trained self-explainers like Activation Oracles remain the stronger baseline. On refusal suppression over 50 prompts, its single committed intervention is slightly below a diff-in-means baseline, and only exceeds it when allowed the best of five attempts. Results are stable across five runs and across model choices for the agents. We also release the pruned subgraphs and context-specific feature readings that revise existing global labels, and invite future work to develop evaluations that can measure their usefulness directly.

papers.title: Fidelity Collapses with Table Size, Not Turn Count: Delivery Architecture in a Deployed Tool-Using Agent
papers.abstract: When a multi-turn agent delivers a tool's structured records into the model's context and re-emits them each turn, every turn can corrupt data the tool computed correctly. We measure this in a production award-travel agent: two architectures over identical frozen payloads, lineage-matched prompts and sampling, differing only in delivery architecture. SYNTHESIS feeds full record sets into the planner's context and answers follow-ups in-head; BYPASS, the deployed system, keeps records in session state, translates follow-ups into arguments for a deterministic filter, and delivers rows over a typed side channel. Across 24 dialogues (339 scored turns per condition), BYPASS scores 92.3% of turns fully correct, SYNTHESIS 45.7% (paired gap +46.6pp [+35.7, +57.1]). Varying delivered-table size by capture date, SYNTHESIS collapses from near-perfect at 10 rows or fewer to 8% or less beyond about 74 rows. On a content-controlled prefix ladder the collapse threshold orders by model capability, from under 10 rows (GPT-4o-mini) to about 198 or more (Gemini 2.5 Pro), while BYPASS stays size-flat for all four models. The collapse is expensive: beyond 100 rows, where almost no SYNTHESIS answer is correct, each correct one costs roughly 200x BYPASS's flat \$0.012. Practitioners converged on typed side-channel delivery for rendering, not correctness; we show it was, unknowingly, also a correctness decision.

papers.title: Quantiles, Not Points: Streaming Quantile Matching for Ordinal-Aware LLM-as-a-Judge Calibration
papers.abstract: LLM-as-a-judge scores are often distributionally shifted from human ratings on any given evaluation task, and post-hoc calibration (mapping LLM to human scores in a small labeled anchor set) has become a popular method to correct for this shift. In this paper we derive the calibration from two positions: that LLMaJ scores are ordinal ratings drawn from a distribution rather than isolated points. We present streaming quantile matching (SQM), a version of a classical method not previously bench marked for LLMaJ calibration, which is built on the two positions by computing the optimal-transport map between the LLM and human score distributions. We develop an evaluation framework and within it we show that unlike point-wise calibrations, SQM respects the ordinality of the human anchor set and achieves the best distributional fidelity and the top overall rank across models and data. We also show that in general, post-hoc calibration narrows the raw error gap between smaller and larger judge models, which opens the possibility of more efficient LLM judges.

papers.title: From Lookups to Lessons: Turning Retrieved Knowledge into Parametric Memory
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) helps large language models (LLMs) answer factual questions beyond their training data, but it adds storage and inference costs. Distilling previously retrieved information into parametric memories enables reuse without online retrieval. However, training the memory to mimic a retriever rewards accurate independent predictions, which do not necessarily improve the final output quality when combined with the LLM's existing predictions. To address this, we introduce ResMem, in which the LLM reads retrieved text offline to generate teacher targets. This design avoids storing massive token representations, unlike existing parametric memory approaches such as MLP Memory, which relies on k-nearest neighbor (kNN) datastores. Furthermore, by using the LLM as an offline teacher that reads privileged retrieved evidence alongside the input, we train a parametric memory to learn an additive logit residual. This residual aligns the predictions of a student sharing the same backbone with the teacher distribution, while self-distillation updates remain confined to the parametric memory. On a Wikipedia subset, ResMem reduces the storage retained for teacher construction by 94.7% compared with the evaluated kNN pipeline. Across five question answering datasets, ResMem raises mean token F1 from 32.83% for the frozen LLM to 34.48%. It also breaks 21% fewer of the LLM's correct answers than a kNN-trained memory. These findings validate our motivation of treating retrieval as a learning resource, with parametric memory shaped by how retrieved knowledge is used to inform the model's future predictions. Code and model weights are available at https://github.com/SSRand/From-Lookups-to-Lessons and https://huggingface.co/RandHan/ResMem-Mistral-7B-v0.3.

papers.title: From Small to Large: Assessing Medical Reasoning, Benchmark Contamination, and Model Size in Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) now answer medical exam questions at or above expert level, but it is unclear whether such scores reflect clinical competence, or are instead affected by the format of the questions being asked (e.g., multiple-choice versus open-ended), prior exposure to the benchmarks, and the difficulty of the questions. These benchmarks are also public and widely used online, which may be resulting in LLM memorization. Models may perform better on questions that they have seen before. It is also not evident whether smaller models, which are more locally deployable in HIPAA-compliant hospital settings, have achieved human performance. In this study, we evaluate fourteen current models from six leading providers, one smaller and one larger model from each provider with two additional open-weight models, on 3,076 questions from four medical benchmarks (MedQA-USMLE, MedMCQA, PubMedQA, and MedBullets) under standard multiple choice, the same questions with the answer choices withheld, and reconstruction of a hidden question from its choices alone. In the standard multiple-choice setting, the strongest models exceed the human-expert baseline on MedQA-USMLE and PubMedQA, but the smaller models trail their larger models by 8.7 percentage points and only two of the six pass the human-expert bar on the licensing examination. Withholding the answer choices, however, makes every model struggle: mean accuracy falls from 82.3% to 50.9%, and the two largest drops belong to the medically specialised models. On memorization, the strongest models reconstruct one question in four from the answer choices alone, yet accuracy holds on the questions they cannot reconstruct. We further weigh accuracy against inference cost and test whether ensembling several models improves medical question answering.

papers.title: Steering Readerly Dynamics: Trajectory-Guided Story Generation with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate stories, but these stories struggle to reproduce engaging readerly dynamics, the evolving reader responses that shape narrative experience. To address this challenge, we propose a framework that learns readerly dynamics from high-quality human-written stories and uses them to guide story generation. Instead of directly modeling high-dimensional story content, we train a small LLM to predict future reader responses as low-dimensional trajectories. We then leverage the strong instruction-following capability of a larger, off-the-shelf writer LLM to generate story segments that follow these predicted trajectories within a given story setting. Our framework improves trajectory-based fidelity to human-written stories by 12%-35% while largely preserving story coherence.

papers.title: Spotting the Artificial: Dialogic Humor Improvisation in Humans and LLMs
papers.abstract: We propose a methodology for investigating the differences between natural and synthetic language in a challenging setting: humorous improvisational dialogue. Our experimental setting compares human-produced comedy improvisations with the dialogues generated by LLMs in a multi-agent environment that we designed. The analysis combines automated linguistic measures with manual annotation grounded in Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL). The results show that, although LLMs can create coherent and creative scenes, they often fail to reproduce key characteristics of spontaneous spoken interaction. In addition, LLM-generated interactions display a strong tendency toward politeness and positive evaluations, contrasting with the broader range of attitudes found in human humorous improvisation. Our evidence highlights both the strengths and limitations of current LLMs in modeling dialogic humor and demonstrate the value of integrating linguistic theory with NLP methods for the analysis of machine-generated language

papers.title: Swap, Replicate, Read the Mass: A Protocol for Auditing Demographic Bias in System One Decision Models
papers.abstract: System One decision models replace text generation with typed, probability-scored answers and are entering production. Answers execute without a person in the loop, and no multi-model audit exists on established bias benchmarks. We provide that audit: three benchmarks: BBQ (all eleven categories), CrowS-Pairs, and SilverSpoon, adapted to the typed interface, twelve models plus a no-thinking ablation, and 1,638,000 decisions. Every order-sensitive item runs twice with options swapped; native typed models also swap labels; ten configurations repeat under extra seeds and batch 16. We find widespread stereotype alignment, order-dependent answers, and confidence that tracks instability rather than bias. In BBQ, 97 of 143 model-by-category scores are significant and 94 aligned, while the commercial reference abstains on 99.5% of ambiguous items, hiding aligned probability mass. Option swaps flip 0.0% to 72.6% of choices; typed scoring stays below 10% except Laya (22-33%), and untuned letter prompting reaches 73%. CrowS-Pairs preference spans 0.496 to 0.816, and boolean answers can be decided by position (1.00 versus 0.005). SilverSpoon judgments shift toward lower-SES labels in five of eight decision models, inherited from the 9B backbone or induced by tuning. Audits must permute options and reverse questions by default; order-invariant scoring should become a procurement requirement.

papers.title: Robustness Starts with the Objective: Designing and Certifying Robust LLM-Generated Heuristics
papers.abstract: LLMs are increasingly used to design heuristics for computer systems. However, most synthesis frameworks evaluate candidates by their average performance, which can mask severe regressions on specific workloads. Even adding adversarial training inputs doesn't eliminate these regressions, and percentile objectives (e.g., optimizing for the 95th percentile) overlook how severe regressions can be beyond the selected threshold. We present TAILOR, a framework that guides LLM synthesis using the Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) of the cost difference between each candidate and an existing baseline on the same workload. This paired CVaR measures the average difference over the worst fraction of workloads. We show that a negative paired CVaR guarantees improvements in both average performance and tail optimality gap relative to the unknown optimum, without ever computing that optimum. We find that TAILOR achieves the best mean--tail trade-off among the synthesis objectives we evaluate across three case studies: Azure GPU batch admission, Azure VM packing, and server placement. Tested across seven diverse optimization benchmarks, TAILOR produces heuristics that are certified with 99% confidence to improve both average performance and tail optimality gaps over the baseline in six of them. On these six benchmarks, TAILOR also outperforms known robust, human-designed alternatives in the tail while achieving better or comparable average-performance improvement over the baseline.

papers.title: AStockArena: Beyond Returns, Can We Entrust Real Capital to the Decisions of Financial Agents?
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in dynamic financial trading, yet real-time trading benchmarks mainly evaluate agents by cumulative returns and risk-adjusted performance. Such outcome metrics cannot show whether trades are faithfully reported, supported by available evidence, and consistent with account states. We introduce AStockArena, a real-time decision-auditing benchmark for continuous trading in China's A-share market. Under shared market conditions and execution constraints, we evaluate 13 open- and closed-source models over 3,198 sequential decisions. AStockArena reconstructsthe actions actually posted to accounts by aligning reports, trade requests, execution responses, and account states, and audits them with eight checks spanning execution traceability (O), evidence sufficiency (RK), and financial meta-awareness (B), combining record verification with consensus expert annotation. Of 1,070 trading points, 72.99% exhibit at least one audit gap; model-level rates range from52.2% to 91.2%, with evidence gaps most prevalent. Historical trade-filtering replay further shows thatportfolio outcomes are sensitive to these flagged trades. Decision-process auditing thus offers a verifiable complement to return-based evaluation of financial agents.

papers.title: Agentic Context Management for Multi-Turn Human-AI Conversations
papers.abstract: LLMs degrade in multi-turn conversation partly because of context pollution: the model's own earlier outputs stay in context and anchor later turns, so an early misreading of the user's intent can persist after the user corrects it. Assistant omission (AO), dropping every assistant message, removes this pollution but fails when interaction is referential: later turns refer back to drafts, decisions, and tool-call results that exist only in assistant turns. We propose Agentic Conversation Context Curation (AC3), a training-free method in which a separate analyzer (1) consolidates the task specification from the user's messages alone, (2) audits the assistant's prior outputs against it, and (3) edits the context, either appending the analysis or discarding the assistant side and rebuilding the context from the specification. A second finding: pollution is contagious. An analyzer that sees the assistant's reasoning while extracting the specification can do worse than no intervention, and instructing it to ignore them did not close the gap, so we exclude assistant turns structurally. On Lost in Conversation (replaying difficulty-selected instances), where AO is an oracle by construction, AC3 closes 55-84% of the gap between full context and AO on three of four tasks and exceeds AO on the fourth, and an LLM that faithfully summarizes the history does not reproduce the gain even with more compute. On real WildChat conversations, a GPT-5-mini judge prefers AC3's next turn over both full context and AO in every configuration of our main table, though this preference depends on the judge; on CollabLLM results are mixed. In stateful tool use (tau2-bench), AO collapses to 0% on every model; AC3 does not collapse, though it falls slightly behind full context. Detector studies show that Reset removes injected pollution but is not span-selective: the gain comes from rebuilding the specification.

papers.title: Dual-Axis Policy Entailment: A Benchmark for Policy-Change Reasoning
papers.abstract: Whether a policy shifts domains and, by extension, continues, broadens, narrows, or reverses previous policy is of paramount importance to the study of public policy. We propose Dual-Axis Policy Entailment (DAPE), which evaluates an ordered pair of policy directives on both dimensions at once: a binary judgment determines whether the two directives govern the same policy domain, and a five-way judgment determines whether the later directive continues, broadens, narrows, or reverses the earlier policy, or governs a different domain altogether. Read together, the two judgments form one five-category label, our primary metric. The two-axis design captures two central dimensions of policy change without conflating errors on either dimension into a generic "irrelevant" label, and it makes annotation more rigorous: a coder cannot dismiss a difficult pair as domain-irrelevant without an explicit, checkable decision. We introduce an expert-annotated benchmark of 1,000 ordered directive pairs drawn from a large corpus of Chinese government policy, together with an annotation-calibration protocol (an adjudication packet with pre/post agreement measurement) that we contribute as a methodological artifact. Fourteen open-weight models and four frontier API flagships fail the task zero-shot: even the best frontier flagship's chance-corrected agreement with expert labels is far below the human ceiling (Cohen's $\kappa \approx 0.29$ vs. $0.53$). A fine-tuned open-weight model (LoRA SFT of Qwen3-14B, five-fold cross-validation) closes this gap, reaching the coder-mutual human ceiling ($\kappa = 0.524$ vs. $0.527$). Finally, we apply our method to China's AI policy (1980-2024) and map the direction of policy change across eras.

papers.title: Skill++: Towards Lifelong Agents via Routing-Aware Skill Refinement
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents extend their capabilities with skills, each with a name, a description, and a body. Under progressive disclosure, an LLM router selects skills by name and description alone and loads only the selected bodies. Skill libraries grow continually as users and agents add new skills. Because the router relies on this metadata, a similar new skill can displace an earlier one, breaking previously correct routing even though the earlier skill and the router are unchanged. This routing interference is aggravated for public skills, whose descriptions may not match their bodies. We formulate the problem as lifelong skill routing, a class-incremental continual learning problem. A solution must keep earlier skills selectable without suppressing new ones. Existing approaches fall short, since continually retraining the router risks catastrophic forgetting and rewriting methods either ignore similar skills or require per-skill feedback. We therefore propose Skill++, which rewrites only the name and description of each incoming skill, without router training or labeled data. The new description states what the body supports, how the skill differs from its closest predecessor, and what related work it excludes. As a library grows to 731 skills over ten sessions, Skill++ selects all required skills for 76.3% of queries, versus 36.4% under the original metadata. Across three benchmarks and five LLM routers, it outperforms all compared approaches, and its gains carry over to the Codex CLI agent harness.

papers.title: Distinguishing among reasoning levels of GPT 5.5 Pro via a grammar lens benchmark
papers.abstract: Does the level of test-time processing effort affect a language model's computational capability? A formal grammar-lens benchmark method, derived from the theory of computation, generates novel data at specified levels, each successively more computationally powerful than the levels below. Using this data, we tested GPT-5.5, and GPT-5.5-Pro-Medium, -High, and -XHigh, showing incrementally increased acceptance of test data: 16, 40, 43, and 52\%, respectively, illustrating the benchmark's ability to discern fine-grained differences among models' added test-time reasoning levels. Additionally, as test-time compute effort increases, model responses diverge from human responses to the same data. This increasing disagreement may turn out to be broadly characteristic of more capable language models, introducing the potential of a general capability-versus-alignment conflict.

papers.title: From Apparent Search Gains to Selection Failures: Auditing Test-Time Inference in Structured Workflow Planning
papers.abstract: Test-time search can improve structured planning, but when methods differ in prompts, post-processing, and selection, it is unclear what an observed gain should be attributed to. We study this question on DisasterBench, where models compose typed multi-tool workflows, by decomposing inference into three observable stages: whether a correct workflow is discovered, whether it survives structural validation, and whether it is finally selected. Comparing independent sampling, a nominal tree-search configuration, and multi-operator search under controlled inference budgets on two model families, we find that (i) the nominal tree-search configuration realizes non-adaptive complete-workflow sampling, and independent sampling with its expansion prompt reproduces its candidate discovery without constructing a tree; (ii) structural validation never removes the last correct workflow in our evaluated candidate pools, whereas majority voting leaves a discovered correct workflow unselected on 10-19% of tasks per pool, with an audit confirming substantive tool-choice or information-flow errors in 57 of 60 examined cases; and (iii) a tool-specification-aware verifier recovers some of these losses but overturns more correct decisions than it fixes. Our results motivate auditing realized rather than nominal inference pipelines, and reporting discovery, validity, and selection separately.

papers.title: Saidzoda-Tajik-E5-Large: Fine-Tuning a 560M Embedder for Tajik Retrieval
papers.abstract: Finding the passage that answers a question is the first step of most practical systems built on documents, and for Tajik we found no openly described model for it. We present Saidzoda-Tajik-E5-Large, a Tajik text embedder built from multilingual-e5-large-instruct (560M parameters). We asked our own Tajik language model to write questions for passages from Tajik laws, tax documents, Wikipedia and web text, and trained on 235,140 question and passage pairs for one epoch, with hard negatives chosen by another embedder and English and Russian pairs mixed in so the model would not forget those languages. On laws the model had never seen, the right passage is among the top ten results for 93.6% of questions, up from 80.2%; on tax documents, 94.5% against 82.6%. On Belebele, the one test we have that was written by people, the gain is smaller and not confirmed (92.2% to 95.2%, with touching intervals), and Russian and English do not change. On law and tax questions written in the same style as its training questions, it is tied with Giga-Embeddings-3B, a model five times its size; on Belebele the 3B and 8B models score slightly higher, and only after we fine-tuned them on our data are they clearly ahead. We also report what failed: training in bfloat16 broke the model, and replacing Tajik letters with similar Russian ones did not help. Our law, tax and Wikipedia test questions come from the same model that wrote the training questions, so we treat those scores as an upper limit until questions written by Tajik speakers are available.
